summary: Updates the conceptual sending algorithm in RFC 2461 so that an IPv6 host can share traffic among equivalent routers for different destinations. The original algorithm did not do load sharing and suggested schemes that were problematic in practice. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: If there are several doors out of a room, don't send everyone through just one. This helps a host spread its traffic over several routers.

questions: ipv6 host to router load sharing
how does an ipv6 host choose between multiple routers
why is round robin router selection a problem in ipv6
subtitle: IPv6 hosts with several equivalent routers should spread traffic among them, using a hash of the destination address.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 conceptual sending algorithm does not load-share among equivalent routers, and its suggestions of always picking the first or going round-robin are problematic.
tldr.mechanism: A host that picks among equivalent routers SHOULD use a hash-based scheme that takes at least the destination IP address into account.
tldr.outcome: Traffic for a given destination tends to keep using the same router, even after a cache entry is deleted, as long as the router list stays the same.

facts.label: Hash input
facts.value: At least the destination IP address

today: RFC 4311 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 2461. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Tie-Breaking Problem
sections.content:
In the conceptual sending algorithm in RFC 2461, a host picks a next hop when no destination cache entry exists for an off-link destination, or when the current router is failing. Sometimes several routers are equivalent, and the host must break the tie in some implementation-specific way.

RFC 2461 allows always choosing the same router or cycling round-robin. The RFC calls both problematic: the first gives no load sharing, and round-robin can cause unstable paths and synchronisation among hosts, so that in the worst case load is concentrated on one router at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone always picks the first door, one door is crowded. If everyone takes turns in the same order, they can still crowd one door at a time.

sections.title: Hash-Based Load Sharing
sections.content:
When a host chooses among multiple equivalent routers, it SHOULD support a method that distributes load for different destinations rather than always choosing the same router. A host that does so SHOULD use a hash-based scheme that takes at least the destination IP address into account, such as those in RFC 2991. The memo takes no stance on whether load sharing is on or off by default.

Traffic to a destination uses the same router while the Destination Cache Entry exists. With a hash, it keeps using the same router even if the entry is deleted, as long as the list of equivalent routers is unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The host uses the destination as a recipe to choose a door, so the same destination always gets the same door.

sections.title: When Not to Share
sections.content: The RFC notes that load sharing can be undesirable where one router has enough capacity and a single router makes traffic patterns more predictable, which helps diagnose connectivity problems beyond the first-hop routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes one door is enough, and using only one makes it easier to see what is going wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: If next-hop selection is predictable, an application can create traffic that all hashes the same, enabling a denial-of-service attack on one router. Hashing makes this harder, and the less predictable the hash, the harder it gets. A malicious local application can still bypass the algorithm, for example with raw sockets, so the RFC concludes the mechanism has no significant incremental impact on Internet infrastructure security.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster who knows how doors are chosen could aim everyone at one door. A secret-ish recipe makes that harder.
